claims.text: A machine-learning-accelerated ab initio simulation framework can predict melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, melting-associated volume change, and selected liquid thermodynamic properties across high-entropy alloys.
The framework's predictive capability arises from capturing local atomic disorder and the energy landscape of multicomponent alloys.
Ab initio molecular dynamics can be integrated with machine-learning potentials and calibrated using high-throughput in-situ calorimetry and diffraction.
Controlled atmospheres and temperature ramps spanning melting can ensure near-equilibrium conditions around the melting point.
Complex local atomic disorder and multicomponent interactions govern the relevant energy landscape during the crystalline-to-liquid transition.
Machine-learning potentials can be tailored to represent local disorder and multicomponent interactions through melting.
Machine learning accelerates otherwise computationally intensive ab initio molecular dynamics simulations.
The accelerated simulations can accurately model both solid and liquid alloy phases.
Modeling both phases enables derivation of temperature-dependent free-energy curves.
Melting temperature and latent heat can be computed from the simulated free-energy behavior.
Volume changes at melting can be assessed through variations of the simulation cell.
Predicted melting temperatures will be within roughly ±5% of experimental measurements.
Predicted enthalpies and entropies of fusion will be within approximately ±10% of experimental measurements.
Predicted liquid specific heat and thermal expansion will agree with experimental trends within margins similar to approximately ±10%.
Conventional ab initio simulations without machine-learning acceleration often struggle with efficiency and prediction in the complex energy landscapes of high-entropy alloys.
The proposed method is applicable to high-entropy alloys containing up to seven principal elements when reliable atomistic potentials can be generated.
Differential scanning calorimetry can provide melting temperatures and fusion enthalpies for validation.
Fusion entropy can be derived from measured latent heat and melting temperature.
High-temperature in-situ X-ray diffraction can determine the volume change at melting.
The framework is to be rejected if melting-temperature errors exceed ±5%, or if fusion enthalpy and entropy errors consistently exceed ±10% across at least three alloy compositions.
